planting.note: Tie or glue the rhizome to driftwood, lava rock, or other hardscape with cotton thread or cyanoacrylate gel until roots attach naturally, typically within 3-6 weeks; do not bury the rhizome in substrate, as this causes rot.

directions: Grown fully submersed in freshwater aquaria attached to hardscape rather than planted in substrate; the tough, dark-green, arrowhead-shaped leaves and rhizome are highly resistant to algae fouling and grazing by herbivorous fish, making this one of the most forgiving true aquatic plants sold in the hobby. It thrives under low to medium aquarium lighting and does not require CO2 injection, though growth accelerates modestly with supplemental CO2 and liquid fertilizer. Native to slow, shaded forest streams of West Africa (Cameroon), it tolerates a wide range of water hardness and a pH of roughly 6.0-7.5. Propagate by dividing the horizontal rhizome into sections with at least two to three leaves and re-attaching each piece to new hardscape.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Center for Aquatic and Invasive Plants — Plant Directory

planting.note: Push stem cuttings 1-2 inches into nutrient-rich aquarium substrate, stripping lower leaves first so no foliage is buried; new roots form from the buried nodes within one to two weeks.

directions: A fast-growing background stem plant for freshwater planted aquaria, native to Southeast Asian wetlands, grown submersed with roots anchored in fine nutrient-rich substrate rather than garden soil. It performs well under medium aquarium lighting and appreciates root tab fertilizer plus liquid iron; CO2 injection is not required but produces noticeably denser, more compact growth and richer leaf color. Regularly pinch and replant the tops of tall stems to prevent the lower portions from becoming leggy and to propagate new plants. This species is the legal, non-restricted alternative to the federally listed noxious weed Hygrophila polysperma and is not itself a listed invasive or noxious species.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — East Indian Hygrophila (SS-AGR-411/AG413)

planting.note: Insert stem cuttings 1 inch into fine aquarium gravel or planted-tank substrate in small groups; space groups several inches apart to allow the reddish foliage to fill in as a mid-ground or background mass.

directions: A native wetland stem plant of the southeastern and south-central United States, cultivated submersed in freshwater aquaria as one of the most reliable red-toned planted-tank species. Leaf color shifts from olive-green to coppery red as light intensity increases, so grow under medium to high aquarium lighting for the best coloration; CO2 injection and a nitrogen-limited, iron-rich fertilizing routine intensify the red tones further. It roots readily from stem cuttings pushed into nutrient-rich substrate and tolerates a wide range of water hardness and temperature. Trim and replant stem tops regularly to keep growth bushy rather than leggy.
sources: USDA PLANTS Database — Ludwigia repens plant profile

planting.note: Anchor stem cuttings 1 inch into aquarium substrate in small clusters; the thick, succulent stems are brittle and root best when handled gently and not buried too deeply.

directions: Native to wetlands and slow streams across the southeastern and south-central United States, this thick-stemmed, round-leaved plant is grown fully submersed as a background or mid-ground species in freshwater planted aquaria, not planted in outdoor garden soil. It grows under medium aquarium lighting and does not require CO2 supplementation, though growth is sturdier and more compact with it. The crushed foliage carries a distinctive lemon scent, a useful identifying trait at the aquarium store. Propagate by cutting healthy stem tips and replanting them directly into the substrate; older lower stems tend to defoliate over time and should be trimmed away.
sources: Native Plant Society of Texas — Bacopa caroliniana species notes

planting.note: Plant the bulb horizontally with the top third exposed above nutrient-rich aquarium substrate; burying it completely can cause the bulb to rot before it establishes roots and leaves.

directions: A bulb-forming true aquatic native to lowland streams of Sri Lanka, grown fully submersed in freshwater aquaria as a striking background centerpiece with long, ruffled, strap-shaped leaves. It grows well under medium aquarium lighting and benefits from root tab fertilizer placed near the bulb; CO2 injection is optional but speeds growth. Aponogeton species periodically send up spikes of small white to pale-purple flowers that reach the water surface, and some bulbs enter a brief dormant rest period after flowering during which leaf production slows before resuming. Propagate by removing small bulb offsets that form alongside the parent bulb once established.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Center for Aquatic and Invasive Plants — Plant Directory

planting.note: Tie or glue the rhizome to driftwood or rock with cotton thread or cyanoacrylate gel until new roots grip the surface, usually within a month; never bury the rhizome in substrate, as this causes it to rot.

directions: An epiphytic fern of Southeast Asian streams, grown fully submersed in freshwater aquaria attached to hardscape rather than rooted in substrate; its tough, leathery, dark-green fronds resist grazing fish and algae buildup better than most soft-leaved aquatic plants. It tolerates low light well and does not need CO2 supplementation, making it a mainstay of low-tech planted tanks, though it also grows readily under medium to high light. Small plantlets frequently form along the leaf margins and can be removed and re-attached to new hardscape once they have a few small roots, or the rhizome itself can be cut into sections to propagate additional plants.

planting.note: Plant the crown in nutrient-rich aquarium substrate with the base of the leaves at the surface of the gravel; the extensive root system benefits from root tab fertilizer buried nearby.

directions: Native to marshes, swamps, and pond margins from Texas and Florida north into the Mississippi Valley, this broad-leaved sword plant is grown fully submersed as a background centerpiece in freshwater planted aquaria rather than in outdoor pond soil. It performs best under medium aquarium lighting with a nutrient-rich substrate and benefits from root tab fertilizer, though it tolerates lower light with slower growth. Mature plants regularly send out long horizontal runners that produce plantlets at the nodes, which can be separated once they have several leaves and their own roots and replanted elsewhere in the tank.
sources: USDA PLANTS Database — Echinodorus cordifolius plant profile

planting.note: Rest the cluster of banana-shaped storage tubers on top of the aquarium substrate rather than burying it, with only fine root hairs anchored below; burying the tubers causes them to rot.

directions: Native to spring-fed rivers and calm lakes of the southeastern United States, this small aquatic gets its common name from the cluster of banana-shaped tuberous roots it produces, which stores energy and anchors the plant without needing to be buried in substrate. Grown fully submersed in freshwater aquaria, it produces rounded, olive-green lily-pad-like leaves on long petioles under medium aquarium lighting; if left unpruned, leaves will reach the surface and float, so trim tall petioles regularly to keep the plant as a mid-ground species. It does not require CO2 injection but grows more vigorously with it. Propagate by dividing offshoot tuber clusters away from the main plant once they have their own leaves and roots.
sources: Florida Native Plant Society — Nymphoides aquatica species profile

planting.note: Separate nursery pot portions into small clumps of a few stems each and press the base into fine nutrient-rich aquarium substrate a few inches apart; new lateral shoots will fill the gaps as the clumps establish.

directions: Discovered along the Rio Cristalino in the southern Amazon basin of Brazil, this compact, hardy foreground plant is grown fully submersed in freshwater planted aquaria as a low, bushy carpet or edging plant rather than in garden soil. It tolerates a broader range of light than many carpeting species, from medium to high aquarium lighting, and unlike more demanding carpet plants it does not strictly require CO2 injection, though CO2 and a nutrient-rich substrate produce a denser, lower-growing mat. Established clumps spread slowly by short lateral shoots rather than fast runners, so propagate by dividing rooted side shoots away from the main clump and replanting them nearby to speed carpet coverage.
sources: Tropica Aquarium Plants — Staurogyne repens species profile

planting.note: Separate tissue-culture or potted portions into small tufts and press the roots into fine nutrient-rich aquarium substrate an inch or two apart; the low, creeping stems will interlace to form a continuous mat as they spread.

directions: Native to the streambanks and wet ground of Argentina, Uruguay, and southern Brazil, Monte Carlo is grown fully submersed in freshwater planted aquaria as a dense, low-growing carpet plant rather than in outdoor garden beds. It needs medium to high aquarium lighting and a nutrient-rich fine substrate to carpet well, and while it can survive without CO2 injection, supplemental CO2 dramatically improves its speed and density as a foreground mat compared to growing it without. Its rounded, bright-green leaves and creeping growth habit resemble true baby tears (Soleirolia soleirolii) but it is far easier to keep fully submersed and roots more readily in aquarium substrate. Trim the mat regularly with scissors and replant healthy trimmings to fill in bare patches.
sources: Tropica Aquarium Plants — Micranthemum tweediei 'Monte Carlo' species profile
